title: Elbow, Forearm, Wrist & Hand
summary: Understand how the forearm and hand produce power grip and fine precision movements.

lessons.title: Elbow & Radioulnar Joints: Pronation and Supination

levels.kid:
Your forearm has two long bones. The **radius** is on the thumb side. The **ulna** is on the pinky side.

Your elbow works like a door hinge. It lets your arm bend and straighten.

But your forearm can also twist! Hold out your hand with the palm up, like you are carrying a bowl of soup. That is called **supination**. Now flip your palm down, like you are patting a dog. That is called **pronation**.

When you flip your hand, the ulna mostly stays still. The radius rolls over it, like one stick crossing over another.

A strong muscle in your upper arm, the **biceps**, helps you twist a screwdriver or turn a doorknob.
levels.hs:
The elbow is really three joints sharing one joint capsule:
- **Humeroulnar joint**: the ulna hooks around the humerus. It is a **hinge joint**, allowing flexion (bending) and extension (straightening).
- **Humeroradial joint**: the top of the radius (the **radial head**) touches a rounded knob on the humerus called the capitulum.
- **Proximal radioulnar joint**: the radial head spins inside a notch on the ulna, held by a ring of tissue called the **annular ligament**. This is a **pivot joint**.

A second pivot joint, the **distal radioulnar joint**, sits near the wrist. Together these two joints let the forearm rotate.

**Supination** turns the palm forward or up. **Pronation** turns the palm back or down. In pronation, the radius crosses over the ulna. The ulna stays mostly fixed; the radius swings around it.

Muscles that do the work:
- Supinators: the **supinator** muscle and the **biceps brachii**
- Pronators: **pronator teres** and **pronator quadratus**

A real example: **nursemaid's elbow**. When an adult yanks a toddler up by the hand, the radial head can slip partly out of the annular ligament. The child holds the arm still and refuses to use it. A doctor can usually pop it back with a quick, gentle twist of the forearm.
levels.college:
**Elbow articulations.** The trochlea of the humerus fits the trochlear notch of the ulna (humeroulnar, hinge), while the capitulum meets the concave radial head (humeroradial). The radial head also sits in the **radial notch of the ulna** (proximal radioulnar joint, pivot), encircled by the **annular ligament**, which attaches to the front and back margins of that notch.

**Ligaments.**
- **Ulnar (medial) collateral ligament (UCL)**: anterior, posterior and transverse bands; the anterior band resists valgus stress.
- **Radial (lateral) collateral ligament**: blends into the annular ligament.
- **Quadrate ligament**: from the radial neck to the ulna, tightening at the ends of rotation.

**Carrying angle.** With the elbow extended and the forearm supinated, the forearm angles laterally about 5 to 15 degrees (a valgus angle), usually larger in females. It disappears in flexion and pronation.

**Rotation.** Pronation and supination occur around an axis running from the radial head to the ulnar head. Typical range is roughly 75 to 80 degrees of pronation and 80 to 85 degrees of supination. The **interosseous membrane**, whose fibres run downward and medially from radius to ulna, links the shafts. At the wrist, the **triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC)** stabilizes the distal radioulnar joint.

**Muscles and nerves.**
- **Biceps brachii** (musculocutaneous nerve): most powerful supinator, especially with the elbow flexed near 90 degrees.
- **Supinator** (deep branch of radial nerve): supinates in any elbow position.
- **Pronator teres** (median nerve): two heads; also weakly flexes the elbow.
- **Pronator quadratus** (anterior interosseous nerve, from median): prime pronator, also binds the distal radius and ulna together.
- Elbow flexion: brachialis, biceps, brachioradialis. Extension: triceps.

That is why you turn a screw clockwise (for a right-hander) with the elbow bent: supination is the stronger movement.
levels.phd:
**Load transmission.** In extension, roughly 60% of axial load crosses the humeroradial joint. Force entering the distal radius is partly transferred to the ulna by the **central band** of the interosseous membrane, oriented about 20 to 25 degrees to the ulnar shaft so that proximal migration of the radius tensions it. The membrane, radial head and TFCC form a **longitudinal stabilizing triad**; disruption of all three underlies the **Essex-Lopresti injury**.

**Kinematics.** The rotation axis is not perfectly fixed. During pronation the radius rolls and slides in the sigmoid notch of the ulna, and the radial head translates slightly. Because the radius effectively shortens relative to the ulna as it crosses over, **ulnar variance becomes more positive in pronation**, especially with grip, raising load on the ulnocarpal side. The TFCC's deep (foveal) fibres of the radioulnar ligaments are key DRUJ restraints; dorsal and palmar components tighten at different ends of rotation.

**Valgus stability.** Morrey and colleagues showed the anterior bundle of the UCL is the primary valgus restraint across roughly 30 to 120 degrees of flexion, with the radial head a secondary restraint that becomes critical when the UCL fails. Bony congruity dominates near full extension and deep flexion.

**Lateral stability.** O'Driscoll described **posterolateral rotatory instability**, attributed mainly to the **lateral ulnar collateral ligament**, which arises from the lateral epicondyle and inserts on the supinator crest of the ulna. Its rupture lets the radius and ulna rotate together off the humerus.

**Muscle mechanics.** The biceps' supination moment arm peaks near 90 degrees of flexion, because its insertion on the radial tuberosity winds around the radius; in extension, supinator contributes proportionally more. Pronator quadratus' deep head also acts as a dynamic DRUJ compressor.

**Controversy.** The relative roles of the interosseous membrane's central band versus the distal oblique bundle (present in a portion of forearms) in DRUJ stability remain debated.
levels.expert:
**Functional range.** Morrey's 1981 study defined a functional arc of 30 to 130 degrees of flexion and 50 degrees each of pronation and supination. Later work (for example Sardelli and colleagues, 2011) found that modern tasks such as keyboards and smartphones need more pronation and flexion, so the old targets may underestimate what patients need after trauma or stiffness release.

**Fracture-dislocations.**
- **Monteggia**: ulnar shaft fracture with radial head dislocation. A line through the radial shaft should hit the capitulum on every radiograph; missing this in children leads to chronic dislocation.
- **Galeazzi**: distal radial shaft fracture with DRUJ disruption.
- **Terrible triad**: posterior dislocation plus radial head and coronoid fractures, typically managed by fixing the coronoid, repairing or replacing the radial head, and repairing the lateral ligaments.
- **Essex-Lopresti**: radial head excision without recognizing interosseous membrane injury causes proximal radial migration and wrist pain; radial head preservation or arthroplasty is favoured.

**Nursemaid's elbow.** Meta-analyses suggest **hyperpronation** reduces radial head subluxation more often on the first attempt than supination-flexion, with less pain.

**UCL injuries.** Overhead throwers sustain attritional anterior bundle tears. Frank Jobe's 1974 reconstruction ("Tommy John surgery") uses a tendon graft through ulnar and humeral tunnels; newer **suture-tape augmented repair** suits selected younger athletes with end-avulsions.

**Distal biceps rupture.** Loss mainly of supination strength (often cited near 40%) and less flexion strength; the **hook test** detects an absent tendon. Supinator preserves some supination, especially with the elbow extended.

**Pitfalls.** The posterior interosseous nerve winds through supinator under the arcade of Frohse and is vulnerable in lateral approaches to the radial head; keeping the forearm pronated moves it away from the field.

**Open questions.** Optimal radial head implant sizing (overstuffing causes capitellar wear), management of chronic DRUJ instability, and whether interosseous membrane reconstruction restores longitudinal stability long term remain unsettled.

keyPoints: The elbow has humeroulnar, humeroradial and proximal radioulnar joints in one capsule
The annular ligament holds the radial head against the radial notch of the ulna
In pronation the radius crosses over a largely fixed ulna
Biceps (musculocutaneous) and supinator (deep radial) supinate; pronator teres and quadratus pronate
The anterior band of the UCL resists valgus stress; the radial head is a secondary restraint
Interosseous membrane, radial head and TFCC together give longitudinal forearm stability

test.explain: Biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity, and its supination leverage peaks near 90 degrees of flexion. Brachialis inserts on the ulna and cannot rotate the forearm.

test.explain: The trochlear notch of the ulna hooks around the trochlea, allowing flexion and extension. The radioulnar joints are the pivots.

test.q: In nursemaid's elbow, what happens?
choices: The radial head slips partly out of its ligament
The ulnar nerve is pinched behind the elbow
The biceps tendon tears off the radius
The olecranon breaks during a fall
test.explain: A pull on a toddler's arm lets the radial head sublux through the annular ligament.

test.q: Which structure is the primary restraint against valgus stress at the elbow?
test.explain: The anterior band of the ulnar (medial) collateral ligament resists valgus stress; the radial head is a secondary restraint.

test.q: The carrying angle describes:
choices: A varus tilt of the flexed forearm
The twist of the radius in pronation
A valgus tilt of the extended forearm
The bend of the hand at the wrist

test.q: Which structure stabilizes the distal radioulnar joint?
test.explain: The TFCC, especially its radioulnar ligaments, stabilizes the DRUJ. The other structures act at the elbow.

test.q: Which muscle wraps the upper radius, is supplied by the deep branch of the radial nerve, and turns the palm up in any elbow position?
test.explain: Supinator works whether the elbow is bent or straight, unlike biceps, which is strongest when flexed.

test.explain: Its fibres run downward and medially from radius to ulna, so load on the radius is shared with the ulna.

test.q: Forearm rotation occurs around an axis running from the radial head to the head of the ___.
test.explain: The axis runs obliquely from the proximal radius to the distal ulna.

kidTest.q: Holding a bowl of soup, palm up, is called:
kidTest.explain: Palm up is supination.

kidTest.explain: The radius rolls over the ulna, which mostly stays still.

kidTest.q: Which muscle helps you twist a screwdriver?
kidTest.explain: The biceps in your upper arm helps twist your forearm.

kidTest.explain: The radius is on the thumb side; the ulna is on the pinky side.

advancedTest.q: A patient's ulnar-sided wrist pain worsens with gripping in full pronation. The best mechanical explanation is:
choices: Pronation makes ulnar variance more negative and unloads the TFCC
Pronation slackens the interosseous membrane and shifts load to the elbow
Pronation makes ulnar variance more positive and loads the ulnocarpal side
Pronation moves the rotation axis onto the radial styloid process
advancedTest.explain: As the radius crosses over in pronation it effectively shortens relative to the ulna, raising ulnar variance and ulnocarpal load, especially with grip.

advancedTest.q: After a radial head fracture is treated by excision, the patient develops wrist pain and proximal radial migration. What was most likely missed?
choices: Injury to the interosseous membrane and DRUJ
A tear of the anterior bundle of the UCL
Compression of the posterior interosseous nerve
A tear of the lateral ulnar collateral ligament
advancedTest.explain: This is Essex-Lopresti: with the membrane and DRUJ disrupted, the radial head is the last longitudinal restraint, so excising it lets the radius migrate.

advancedTest.q: After a complete distal biceps rupture, supination strength is tested with the elbow extended and then at 90 degrees. The expected finding is:
choices: No loss in either position because pronator teres takes over
Greater loss in extension, where biceps leverage is highest
Equal loss in both positions because biceps supinates equally
Greater loss at 90 degrees, as supinator partly compensates
advancedTest.explain: Biceps' supination leverage peaks near 90 degrees, while supinator acts in all positions and contributes relatively more in extension.

advancedTest.q: After a UCL tear, a radial head fracture leaves the elbow grossly unstable to valgus stress. Why?
choices: The radial head carries the attachment of the anterior UCL band
The radial head is the secondary valgus restraint once the UCL fails
The radial head transmits most load in deep flexion
The radial head anchors the annular ligament to the olecranon
advancedTest.explain: The anterior UCL band is primary; the radial head becomes the critical secondary restraint when that ligament is torn, so losing both destabilizes the elbow.

lessons.title: Anterior Forearm: The Flexor Layers

levels.kid:
Make a fist and squeeze. Now put your other hand on the inside of your forearm. Feel it get hard? Those are your **flexor muscles** working.

The muscles that bend your fingers are not in your fingers at all. They live in your forearm! They pull on long, strong strings called **tendons**, which run down into your fingers like puppet strings.

These forearm muscles are stacked in layers, like a sandwich. The top layer bends your wrist. The middle layer bends most of your finger joints. The deepest layer bends your fingertips and your thumb tip.

Most of these muscles start from one bony bump on the inside of your elbow. That is why golfers can get a sore elbow there.
levels.hs:
The front of the forearm is the **anterior compartment**. Its muscles mainly **flex** (bend) the wrist and fingers, and some **pronate** the forearm (turn the palm down). Doctors group them into three layers.

- **Superficial layer** (four muscles): pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus and flexor carpi ulnaris. Most of them arise from the **medial epicondyle** of the humerus by a shared **common flexor origin**.
- **Intermediate layer**: one muscle, **flexor digitorum superficialis** (FDS). It bends the middle finger joints.
- **Deep layer** (three muscles): **flexor digitorum profundus** (FDP), which bends the fingertip joints; **flexor pollicis longus**, which bends the thumb tip; and **pronator quadratus**, a square muscle near the wrist.

Two nerves supply this compartment. The **median nerve** supplies most of these muscles. The **ulnar nerve** supplies only flexor carpi ulnaris and the half of FDP that serves the ring and little fingers.

A real example: about 1 in 7 people lack **palmaris longus** on at least one side. You can check by touching your thumb to your little finger and flexing your wrist. A thin tendon pops up in the middle of the wrist if you have it. Surgeons often borrow this tendon as a graft because the hand works normally without it.

Overuse of the common flexor origin causes **medial epicondylitis** (golfer's elbow).
levels.college:
The anterior compartment holds eight muscles in three layers. Its actions are wrist flexion, flexion of the finger and thumb joints, and pronation.

**Superficial layer** (lateral to medial: Pronator teres, Flexor carpi radialis, Palmaris longus, Flexor carpi ulnaris):
- **Pronator teres** has humeral and ulnar heads. It inserts on the midlateral radius and pronates and weakly flexes the elbow. The median nerve usually passes between its two heads.
- **Flexor carpi radialis** (FCR) inserts on the base of the 2nd (and 3rd) metacarpal. It flexes the wrist and abducts it radially. Its tendon is a landmark for the radial artery, which lies just lateral to it.
- **Palmaris longus** blends into the palmar aponeurosis.
- **Flexor carpi ulnaris** (FCU) has humeral and ulnar heads and inserts via the **pisiform** (the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments). The ulnar nerve enters the forearm between its heads.

**Intermediate layer**: **FDS** arises from a humeroulnar head and a radial head. Its four tendons flex the **PIP joints**. Each tendon splits (Camper's chiasm) to let the FDP tendon pass through.

**Deep layer**:
- **FDP** arises from the ulna and interosseous membrane and flexes the **DIP joints**.
- **Flexor pollicis longus** (FPL) arises from the radius and flexes the thumb IP joint.
- **Pronator quadratus** runs between the distal ulna and radius. It is the main pronator when the elbow is not loaded.

**Innervation**:
- The **median nerve** supplies the superficial and intermediate muscles except FCU.
- Its **anterior interosseous branch** supplies FPL, the lateral FDP (index and middle fingers) and pronator quadratus.
- The **ulnar nerve** supplies FCU and the medial FDP (ring and little fingers).

**Clinical tests**: Hold the other fingers extended and flex one finger. Any PIP flexion you see comes from FDS. Hold the PIP joint still and flex the DIP joint to test FDP.
levels.phd:
Developmentally, the flexor-pronator mass comes from the ventral muscle mass of the limb bud. This explains why it is supplied by anterior divisions of the brachial plexus. The median nerve carries C6–T1 fibres and the ulnar nerve carries C8–T1. Segmentally, finger flexion is mainly **C8**, which is why C8 radiculopathy weakens grip.

FDP is a functionally coupled muscle. Its index slip is often partly independent. Its middle, ring and little slips share a common muscle belly and are linked by tendon interconnections. This is the **quadriga effect**: if one FDP tendon is shortened or tethered, as after over-advancement or amputation-stump suturing, the other tendons cannot reach full excursion, and grip weakens across the hand. FDS slips have more independent motor units, so they suit individuated finger control. FDS to the little finger is absent or weak in a notable minority of hands. This makes the isolated FDS test unreliable for that finger.

**Dual innervation of FDP** varies. The usual split is median (via the AIN) to the radial two slips and ulnar to the ulnar two. Still, the ulnar nerve may supply all four slips, or the AIN may supply three. **Martin–Gruber anastomoses** (median-to-ulnar connections in the forearm, often arising from the AIN) occur in a substantial minority of limbs. They complicate how lesions are localized on nerve conduction studies.

Mechanically, the long flexors cross several joints. Wrist position therefore changes their force through the length–tension relationship. Wrist extension stretches the flexors and raises grip force. This is **tenodesis**, the passive finger flexion seen when the wrist is extended. It is used in tetraplegia rehabilitation.

Pronation torque comes mostly from pronator quadratus at low loads. Electromyography shows that pronator teres is recruited during resisted or rapid pronation, especially with the elbow flexed. The deep head of pronator quadratus also acts as a dynamic stabilizer of the distal radioulnar joint.

**Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome** gives purely motor weakness of FPL and index FDP. Patients cannot make an "OK" sign and pinch with a flat tip instead. Many cases are now thought to be neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage–Turner), not compression.
levels.expert:
For a surgeon, the flexor layers are mostly a map of where nerves lie and where they can be trapped.

The **median nerve** passes possible compression points as it travels down the forearm:
- the ligament of Struthers, found with a supracondylar process in roughly 1% of people
- the lacertus fibrosus (bicipital aponeurosis)
- between the two heads of pronator teres
- the proximal arch of FDS (the sublimis bridge)

This is **pronator syndrome**. It causes forearm aching and numbness of the palm. Numbness in the palmar cutaneous branch territory, together with a weak or normal Tinel sign at the wrist, separates it from carpal tunnel syndrome. That branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel. Nerve conduction studies are often normal. Decompression results vary, and the diagnosis remains debated.

The **ulnar nerve** passes under the **Osborne ligament** (the cubital tunnel retinaculum). It then runs through the aponeurosis of FCU and the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis. Exploration must release all these levels.

**Medial epicondylitis** is a tendinosis of the common flexor origin, mostly pronator teres and FCR. Look for coexisting ulnar neuritis. Debridement is reserved for refractory cases.

**Flexor tendon injuries**:
- **Jersey finger** is an avulsion of FDP, usually from the ring finger, caused by forced extension against active flexion. It is classified by Leddy–Packer. Retraction into the palm (type I) threatens the blood supply from the vincula, so repair needs to be early.
- **Volar forearm lacerations** ("spaghetti wrist") need methodical identification of up to 12 tendons plus the median and ulnar nerves. A clue: the median nerve lies deep to palmaris longus. It is yellower and has vasa nervorum on its surface, unlike the glistening tendons.

**Forearm compartment syndrome** most often involves the deep volar compartment. FDP and FPL are at greatest risk. The end result is **Volkmann ischaemic contracture**. Decompression uses a curvilinear volar incision that includes release of the lacertus.

**Nerve transfers** now use the redundancy of this compartment. Examples are a branch to brachialis transferred to the AIN for lower-trunk injuries, and an expendable FDS motor branch used as a donor.

Open questions include the true cause of isolated AIN palsy (constriction or inflammation of nerve fascicles?) and how best to test for pronator syndrome objectively.

keyPoints: Anterior forearm muscles flex the wrist and fingers and pronate the forearm
Three layers: superficial (4 muscles), intermediate (FDS), deep (FDP, FPL, pronator quadratus)
Most superficial muscles arise from the medial epicondyle (common flexor origin)
FDS flexes the PIP joints; FDP flexes the DIP joints
Median nerve supplies most; ulnar nerve supplies FCU and the medial half of FDP
The anterior interosseous nerve supplies FPL, lateral FDP and pronator quadratus

test.q: Most superficial forearm flexors arise from which bony landmark?
test.explain: The common flexor origin is the medial epicondyle. The lateral epicondyle is the common extensor origin.

test.q: Which muscle forms the intermediate layer by itself?
test.explain: FDS is the sole muscle of the intermediate layer. FDP and FPL are deep, and FCR is superficial.

test.q: Which nerve supplies flexor carpi ulnaris?
test.explain: FCU and the medial half of FDP are the ulnar nerve's muscles in the forearm. The median nerve supplies the rest.

test.q: Flexor digitorum profundus mainly flexes which joints?
test.explain: FDP inserts on the distal phalanges and flexes the DIP joints. FDS flexes the PIP joints.

test.q: The anterior interosseous nerve supplies which group?
test.explain: The AIN is a deep median-nerve branch to the three deep-layer targets: FPL, the index/middle FDP slips and pronator quadratus.

test.q: Which muscle is missing on at least one side in about 1 in 7 people?
test.explain: Palmaris longus is often absent, and it is used as a tendon graft because losing it causes no loss of function.

test.q: The FCU tendon inserts by way of which carpal bone?
test.explain: FCU inserts on the pisiform and continues to the hamate and 5th metacarpal through ligaments.

test.q: Overuse injury of the common flexor origin is called:
test.explain: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) affects the flexor-pronator origin. Lateral epicondylitis is tennis elbow of the extensors.

test.q: The median nerve usually enters the forearm by passing between the heads of:
test.explain: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres. The ulnar nerve passes between the heads of FCU.

test.q: The square deep muscle near the wrist that pronates the forearm is pronator ___.
test.explain: Pronator quadratus is the main pronator at low loads.

test.q: What abbreviation is used for flexor digitorum superficialis?
test.explain: FDS flexes the PIP joints. Each of its tendons splits to let an FDP tendon pass through.

test.q: The radial artery lies just lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi ___.
test.explain: The FCR tendon is a landmark for finding the radial pulse.

kidTest.q: Where are most muscles that bend your fingers?
kidTest.explain: They sit in the forearm and pull on long tendons.

kidTest.q: How are the forearm flexor muscles arranged?
kidTest.explain: They are layered like a sandwich.

kidTest.q: What does the top layer mainly bend?
kidTest.explain: The top layer mostly bends the wrist.

kidTest.q: Where do many of these muscles start?
kidTest.explain: They start from a bump on the inner elbow.

kidTest.q: Strong strings joining muscles to bones are called t _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Tendons work like puppet strings for the fingers.

advancedTest.q: A patient cannot flex the thumb IP or index DIP joints but has normal sensation. The most likely site of the lesion is:
choices: Median nerve inside the carpal tunnel
Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel
Medial cord of the brachial plexus
advancedTest.explain: The AIN is purely motor and supplies FPL and the index FDP. A carpal tunnel lesion would spare these muscles and affect sensation.

advancedTest.q: Over-advancing one FDP tendon in repair weakens grip in the neighbouring fingers. This happens because:
choices: The ulnar nerve supplies the four FDP slips
Pronator quadratus anchors the FDP tendons
The FDP slips share a common muscle belly
FDS slips share the same motor branch
advancedTest.explain: This is the quadriga effect. The FDP slips are mechanically linked, so tethering one limits how far the others can move.

advancedTest.q: Forearm aching with numbness over the thenar palm, plus normal wrist conduction, best suggests:
advancedTest.explain: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve before the carpal tunnel. Numbness in its area points to compression higher in the forearm.

advancedTest.q: In tetraplegia rehabilitation, wrist extension is used to produce finger flexion because:
choices: Wrist extensors also insert on the phalanges
Pronator quadratus contracts when the wrist extends
Wrist extension activates the anterior interosseous nerve
Stretching the long flexors creates passive tension
advancedTest.explain: Tenodesis: the multi-joint flexors are lengthened across the wrist, so passive tension flexes the fingers without active contraction.

lessons.title: Posterior Forearm Extensors & the Anatomical Snuffbox

levels.kid:
Make a fist, then open your hand wide. The muscles that open your hand live on the back of your forearm, the hairy side. They are called **extensors**. Extend means to straighten.

These muscles are like puppet strings. The muscle part sits near your elbow. Long, thin ropes called **tendons** run down to your wrist and fingers. When the muscle pulls, the ropes straighten your fingers.

Now stick your thumb out like a hitchhiker. Look at the base of your thumb. Can you see a little dip between two tendons? That is the **anatomical snuffbox**! Long ago, people put a powder called snuff there. Doctors press on this dip when someone falls on their hand. If it hurts, a tiny wrist bone might be broken.
levels.hs:
The back (posterior) side of the forearm holds the **extensor muscles**. They straighten (**extend**) the wrist and fingers and lift the thumb. Almost all of them start from one bony bump on the outside of the elbow, the **lateral epicondyle** of the humerus. Their tendons cross the back of the wrist to reach the hand.

All of these muscles are controlled by one nerve, the **radial nerve**, through its deep branch. If the radial nerve is damaged, a person cannot lift the wrist, so the hand flops down. This is called **wrist drop**.

Three thumb tendons form a landmark you can see on yourself. Stretch your thumb back hard and a small triangular hollow appears at the base of the thumb. This is the **anatomical snuffbox**:
- One side is formed by the tendons of **abductor pollicis longus** and **extensor pollicis brevis**.
- The other side is formed by the tendon of **extensor pollicis longus**.
- The floor contains the **scaphoid** bone, and the **radial artery** crosses it.

Real example: a teenager falls onto an outstretched hand. The X-ray looks normal, but pressing in the snuffbox is very painful. Doctors treat this as a possible **scaphoid fracture**, the most commonly broken carpal bone, until it is proven otherwise. A missed scaphoid fracture can lose its blood supply and fail to heal.
levels.college:
The posterior compartment contains about 12 muscles in **superficial** and **deep** layers. The **radial nerve** supplies them all, mainly through the **posterior interosseous nerve (PIN)**, the continuation of its deep branch after it pierces supinator.

**Superficial layer** (mostly from the lateral epicondyle via the **common extensor origin**):
- Brachioradialis: flexes the elbow, strongest in midpronation; supplied by the radial nerve proper.
- Extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL; also radial nerve proper) and brevis (ECRB).
- Extensor digitorum, extensor digiti minimi, extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU).
- Anconeus: assists elbow extension.

**Deep layer**:
- Supinator: wraps the radius; PIN passes between its two heads.
- Abductor pollicis longus (APL), extensor pollicis brevis (EPB), extensor pollicis longus (EPL).
- Extensor indicis.

**Extensor retinaculum and six compartments** (radial to ulnar):
1. APL + EPB
2. ECRL + ECRB
3. EPL, which turns around **Lister's tubercle**
4. Extensor digitorum + extensor indicis (with PIN terminal branch)
5. Extensor digiti minimi
6. ECU

On the fingers, extensor digitorum tendons form the **extensor expansion (dorsal hood)**. They are linked by juncturae tendinum, which is why the ring finger is hard to extend alone.

**Anatomical snuffbox**:
- Radial (palmar) border: APL and EPB.
- Ulnar (dorsal) border: EPL.
- Floor: scaphoid and trapezium, with the radial styloid proximally.
- Contents: the **radial artery** running toward the first dorsal interosseous space; the cephalic vein begins nearby, and superficial radial nerve branches cross the roof.

Clinical anchors: wrist drop (radial nerve at the spiral groove), **lateral epicondylitis** ("tennis elbow", ECRB origin), and **de Quervain tenosynovitis** (first compartment).
levels.phd:
**Innervation hierarchy.** The radial nerve divides near the lateral epicondyle, at about the radiocapitellar joint level, into the superficial (sensory) branch and the deep branch. Brachioradialis and ECRL are supplied above this division. ECRB is variable: it is often supplied by the deep branch, but sometimes by the superficial branch. The deep branch passes under the **arcade of Fröhse**, the fibrous proximal edge of the superficial head of supinator, and becomes the PIN. Its sequential motor branches run roughly supinator, extensor digitorum, EDM, ECU, then APL, EPL, EPB and extensor indicis. This order explains graded deficits: a PIN lesion spares ECRL, so the wrist still extends but **deviates radially**, and the patient has finger and thumb drop without sensory loss.

**Biomechanics.** The wrist extensors act as synergists in power grip. Contracting them extends the wrist to optimize length-tension in the long finger flexors; a flexed wrist weakens grip markedly. ECRB, which inserts on the base of the third metacarpal, is the most central wrist extensor. It is the main tendon transfer target, and its origin is the main site of enthesopathy.

**Lateral epicondylitis** is histologically an **angiofibroblastic tendinosis** (Nirschl): disorganized collagen with neovascularization and little inflammatory infiltrate. This challenges the "-itis" label and the traditional anti-inflammatory rationale.

**Snuffbox and scaphoid vascularity.** The scaphoid is supplied mainly by dorsal carpal branches of the radial artery entering at the dorsal ridge, retrograde from distal to proximal (Gelberman and Menon, 1980). These vessels supply roughly 70-80% of the bone, including the proximal pole. Proximal fractures therefore risk **avascular necrosis** and nonunion. Snuffbox tenderness is sensitive but poorly specific. It is usually combined with scaphoid tubercle tenderness and pain on axial thumb compression to raise specificity.

**First compartment variation.** APL commonly has multiple slips, and EPB often runs in a separate subsheath within the first compartment. Failure to release this subsheath is a recognized cause of persistent de Quervain symptoms after surgery.
levels.expert:
**Distinguishing radial neuropathies.** A key bedside distinction is **PIN syndrome** versus **radial tunnel syndrome**. PIN syndrome causes motor weakness with no sensory loss. Radial tunnel syndrome is a contested entity of lateral forearm pain, often without objective weakness or EMG changes, and it is easily confused with refractory lateral epicondylitis. The two can coexist. Tenderness about 4-5 cm distal to the epicondyle over supinator, and pain on resisted middle-finger extension, point toward radial tunnel pathology. Space-occupying lesions can also compress the PIN in nontraumatic palsy: lipomas, ganglia, or rheumatoid synovitis of the radiocapitellar joint. Ultrasound or MRI is warranted before attributing the palsy to entrapment. In Monteggia fracture-dislocations, a dislocated radial head can stretch the PIN.

**Tendon pathology pitfalls.**
- **EPL rupture** around Lister's tubercle occurs weeks after even nondisplaced distal radius fractures, from attrition and watershed ischemia. The usual repair is **extensor indicis to EPL transfer**.
- **Intersection syndrome** is friction where the first-compartment muscle bellies cross the ECRL and ECRB tendons, about 4-8 cm proximal to the wrist. Rowers are typical. It can be mistaken for de Quervain tenosynovitis.
- Rheumatoid **Vaughan-Jackson syndrome** is sequential ulnar-to-radial extensor ruptures over a prominent distal ulna.

**Tendon transfers for high radial palsy.** Standard schemes use pronator teres to ECRB for the wrist, flexor carpi radialis or flexor carpi ulnaris to extensor digitorum for the fingers, and palmaris longus to rerouted EPL for the thumb. These transfers rely on the principle that donor muscles of matched excursion and synergy can be retrained.

**Scaphoid imaging.** Up to about a fifth of scaphoid fractures are occult on initial radiographs. Early **MRI** is now favored over serial X-rays: it has high sensitivity, detects alternative injuries, and cuts unnecessary immobilization. CT better defines displacement and union. Proximal pole and displaced waist fractures increasingly go to percutaneous or open screw fixation. Established nonunion with avascular necrosis may need vascularized bone graft, such as the 1,2-intercompartmental supraretinacular artery graft (Zaidemberg) harvested from the dorsal radius. That graft depends directly on the snuffbox-region vascular anatomy.

**Procedural caution.** Snuffbox (distal radial) arterial access is used for coronary angiography, with lower reported rates of radial artery occlusion. The superficial radial nerve crossing the roof is at risk, as it is in first-compartment release; injury can cause painful neuromas.

keyPoints: Posterior forearm muscles extend the wrist, fingers and thumb
Most arise from the lateral epicondyle (common extensor origin)
All are supplied by the radial nerve, mostly via the posterior interosseous nerve
Extensor retinaculum holds tendons in six dorsal compartments
Snuffbox: APL and EPB on one side, EPL on the other; scaphoid in floor, radial artery inside
Snuffbox tenderness after a fall suggests scaphoid fracture, which risks avascular necrosis

test.explain: The radial nerve, mostly through its deep branch (posterior interosseous nerve), supplies all posterior compartment muscles.

test.q: Most superficial extensors share an origin on the:

Vessels enter distally and flow backward
Vessels enter proximally and flow distally
The ulnar artery is cut by the fall

On the palm of the hand

Long finger flexors are too short to pull well
The extensor tendons rupture under load

advancedTest.explain: Attritional EPL rupture at Lister's tubercle is classically treated with an extensor indicis transfer.

advancedTest.q: Histology showing angiofibroblastic tendinosis in tennis elbow most directly challenges:
choices: The use of ECRB as the transfer target
A primarily inflammatory model of disease
The radial supply of the extensors
The lateral epicondyle as the origin

lessons.title: Carpal Bones, Carpal Tunnel & Guyon's Canal

levels.kid:
Your wrist is not one bone. It is made of **eight small bones**, packed together like pebbles in a little bag. They let your hand bend and twist in many directions.

On the palm side, these bones make a curved groove, like a tiny tunnel. A strong band of tissue stretches across the top like a roof. This is the **carpal tunnel**. Through it pass the cords that bend your fingers, plus one important nerve called the **median nerve**.

Nearby is a smaller tunnel on the pinky side, called **Guyon's canal**. The **ulnar nerve** goes through it.

If a tunnel gets squeezed, the nerve inside gets pinched. Then fingers can tingle, like when your foot falls asleep.
levels.hs:
The wrist, or **carpus**, contains **eight carpal bones** in two rows of four. A classic memory aid, going from the thumb side outward and then back, is "Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle."
- **Proximal row** (thumb to pinky): scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform
- **Distal row** (thumb to pinky): trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate

The **scaphoid** is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, usually from a fall on an outstretched hand.

On the palm side, the carpal bones form a concave arch. The **flexor retinaculum** (transverse carpal ligament) bridges this arch and turns it into the **carpal tunnel**. Ten structures pass through: the **median nerve** and nine flexor tendons (four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus, and flexor pollicis longus).

**Carpal tunnel syndrome** happens when pressure in the tunnel compresses the median nerve. People get numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger, often at night. Severe cases weaken the thumb muscles.

**Guyon's canal** (the ulnar tunnel) is a separate passage on the little-finger side, between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate. It carries the **ulnar nerve and ulnar artery**, which pass superficial to the flexor retinaculum, not through the carpal tunnel.
levels.college:
**Carpal bones.** The proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform) articulates with the distal radius and the articular disc of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) at the radiocarpal joint. The ulna does not articulate directly with the carpus. The **pisiform** is a sesamoid within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon. The distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate) meets the metacarpals; the **capitate** is the largest carpal bone. The saddle-shaped trapezium–first metacarpal joint gives the thumb its mobility.

**Scaphoid blood supply.** Branches of the radial artery enter mainly distally and dorsally, so blood flows **retrograde** toward the proximal pole. Waist fractures can therefore cause **avascular necrosis** of the proximal pole. Snuffbox tenderness with normal X-rays still warrants immobilization or further imaging.

**Carpal tunnel.** The flexor retinaculum attaches to four pillars:
- Radially: scaphoid tubercle and trapezium tubercle
- Ulnarly: pisiform and hook of hamate

Contents: median nerve (most superficial, radial side), FDS ×4, FDP ×4, FPL. FDS and FDP share the **common flexor sheath** (ulnar bursa). FPL has its own sheath (radial bursa). Flexor carpi radialis runs in a separate split of the retinaculum, so it is not a tunnel content.

**Median nerve in the hand.** The **recurrent (thenar) branch** supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and superficial flexor pollicis brevis. The **palmar cutaneous branch** arises proximal to the wrist and passes **superficial** to the retinaculum. That is why carpal tunnel syndrome typically spares sensation over the thenar eminence.

**Guyon's canal.** Its floor is the retinaculum and pisohamate ligament. Its roof is the volar carpal ligament and palmaris brevis. It runs between the pisiform and the hook of hamate. Within it, the ulnar nerve divides into superficial (mostly sensory) and deep (motor) branches. The **dorsal cutaneous branch** of the ulnar nerve leaves proximal to the canal, so dorsal-hand sensation is spared in Guyon's canal lesions.
levels.phd:
**Carpal kinematics.** The proximal row is an **intercalated segment**: no tendons insert on it except FCU via the pisiform, so its motion is dictated by ligaments and articular geometry. The scaphoid tends to flex under load and the triquetrum to extend. The **scapholunate interosseous ligament** (dorsal portion strongest) and lunotriquetral ligament balance these opposing tendencies. SL disruption lets the lunate extend with the triquetrum, producing **dorsal intercalated segment instability (DISI)**. LT disruption produces volar (VISI) patterns. Untreated SL injury progresses to **SLAC (scapholunate advanced collapse)** arthritis in a predictable sequence, first radial styloid–scaphoid, then capitolunate. The radiolunate joint is relatively preserved, which is the basis of salvage operations. Mayfield's classic cadaver work described progressive perilunar instability, extending from radial to ulnar around the lunate and ending in lunate dislocation.

**Carpal tunnel pressure physiology.** Normal resting pressure is low, a few mmHg. It rises several-fold in full flexion or extension. Gelberman and colleagues showed elevated pressures in CTS patients. Epineurial venous flow is impaired at roughly 20–30 mmHg, and axonal transport and conduction fail at higher pressures. Chronic compression causes demyelination, then axonal loss, with synovial fibrosis of the flexor tenosynovium. Risk associations include pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly and **transthyretin amyloidosis**.

**Variation.** The thenar branch may be extraligamentous (most common), subligamentous, or **transligamentous**, piercing the retinaculum, which matters during division. Other variants include a persistent median artery, a bifid median nerve, and lumbrical origins that extend into the tunnel during finger flexion.

**Guyon's canal zones** (Gross and Gelberman):
- **Zone 1**, proximal to the bifurcation: mixed motor and sensory deficit
- **Zone 2**, deep branch: pure motor, often from ganglion or hook of hamate fracture
- **Zone 3**, superficial branch: pure sensory

A deep-branch lesion distal to the hypothenar branches spares hypothenar muscles but weakens the interossei and adductor pollicis. Clawing is **more** pronounced than in proximal ulnar lesions because FDP to the ring and little fingers is intact (the **ulnar paradox**).
levels.expert:
**Diagnosing CTS.** The diagnosis is clinical, supported by tests. Phalen's and Tinel's signs have modest accuracy. **Durkan's carpal compression test** and a hand diagram (Katz) perform better. Validated tools such as the CTS-6 score combine findings like nocturnal symptoms, median-distribution numbness, thenar atrophy, two-point discrimination, Phalen's and Tinel's. Nerve conduction studies show prolonged distal motor and sensory latencies and comparison abnormalities, for example median–ulnar ring-finger latency difference. Normal studies do not exclude mild CTS. **Ultrasound** cross-sectional area of the median nerve at the tunnel inlet is increasingly used. Always consider mimics: C6/C7 radiculopathy, pronator syndrome (which involves the palmar cutaneous territory), thoracic outlet syndrome and peripheral neuropathy. Double-crush is debated.

**Treatment and surgical pitfalls.** Mild cases respond to neutral night splinting and steroid injection. Injection relief also predicts surgical success. **Carpal tunnel release**, open or endoscopic (Agee single-portal, Chow two-portal), divides the transverse carpal ligament along the ring-finger ray axis, ulnar to the palmaris longus line. This keeps away from the thenar branch and the palmar cutaneous branch. Kaplan's cardinal line helps localize the motor branch and the superficial palmar arch. Long-term outcomes are similar between techniques. Endoscopic release offers earlier return to work but carries a small risk of nerve injury. Incomplete distal release is the commonest cause of persistent symptoms. **Pillar pain** is typical after release. Acute CTS after distal radius fracture or perilunate dislocation needs **urgent** decompression.

**Guyon's canal in practice.** Space-occupying lesions predominate: ganglia, hook of hamate nonunion (golfers, batters), ulnar artery aneurysm or thrombosis (**hypothenar hammer syndrome**), and anomalous muscles. Cyclists develop deep-branch neuropathy from handlebar pressure. Image with CT for hamate hook fractures and MRI or ultrasound for masses. Release opens the volar carpal ligament and decompresses the deep motor branch around the hamate hook.

**Open questions.** Several issues are unsettled: the role of ultrasound-guided percutaneous release; occupational causation, since keyboard use is only weakly linked; whether bilateral CTS should prompt screening for cardiac amyloid; and the best timing of surgery in diabetic neuropathy.

keyPoints: Eight carpal bones in two rows: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate
Scaphoid has retrograde blood supply, so waist fractures risk proximal pole necrosis
Flexor retinaculum spans scaphoid/trapezium and pisiform/hamate to form the carpal tunnel
Carpal tunnel holds the median nerve plus 9 tendons (FDS ×4, FDP ×4, FPL)
Palmar cutaneous branch runs superficial to the tunnel, so thenar skin is spared in CTS
Guyon's canal (pisiform–hamate hook) carries ulnar nerve and artery; lesions sorted into 3 zones

test.q: Which carpal bone is most commonly fractured?
test.explain: The scaphoid usually breaks in a fall on an outstretched hand. The lunate is more often dislocated than fractured.

test.q: Which bones form the ulnar boundaries of Guyon's canal?
test.explain: Guyon's canal runs between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate on the little-finger side.

test.q: How many tendons pass through the carpal tunnel?
test.explain: Nine tendons pass through: four FDS, four FDP and FPL. Together with the median nerve, that makes ten structures.

test.q: Which structure travels through Guyon's canal rather than the carpal tunnel?
test.explain: The ulnar nerve and artery pass superficial to the flexor retinaculum in Guyon's canal.

test.q: Why is thenar skin sensation usually normal in carpal tunnel syndrome?
choices: The recurrent branch carries the thenar skin fibers
The palmar cutaneous branch runs superficial to the tunnel
The radial nerve takes over thenar skin after compression
The ulnar nerve supplies the skin of the thenar region
test.explain: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve proximal to the wrist and passes over the retinaculum, so it escapes compression.

test.q: Why can a scaphoid waist fracture lead to avascular necrosis?
choices: The scaphoid has no blood vessels after childhood
The fracture blocks venous drainage to the radius
Blood enters distally and flows back to the proximal pole
The ulnar artery is torn in most such fractures
test.explain: Retrograde supply means a waist fracture can cut off the proximal pole's blood flow.

test.q: Which tendon runs in its own split of the retinaculum, outside the carpal tunnel?
test.explain: FCR runs in a separate compartment. FPL, FDS and FDP are tunnel contents.

test.q: Which proximal-row bone is a sesamoid within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon?
test.explain: The pisiform lies inside the FCU tendon. The hamate is in the distal row.

test.q: Which muscle is supplied by the recurrent (thenar) branch of the median nerve?
test.explain: The recurrent branch supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and superficial FPB. The other options are ulnar-innervated.

test.q: The flexor ___ (transverse carpal ligament) forms the roof of the carpal tunnel.
test.explain: The flexor retinaculum bridges the carpal arch and turns it into a tunnel.

test.q: Name the largest carpal bone, which sits in the distal row.
test.explain: The capitate is the largest carpal bone and sits centrally in the distal row.

test.q: Which nerve is compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome?
test.explain: The median nerve is the only nerve inside the carpal tunnel.

kidTest.q: How many small bones are in your wrist?
kidTest.explain: The wrist has eight carpal bones.

kidTest.q: What passes through the carpal tunnel?
choices: The long bone of your upper arm
Air and some drops of water
kidTest.explain: Finger tendons and the median nerve go through it.

kidTest.q: Which nerve goes through Guyon's canal?
kidTest.explain: The ulnar nerve uses the tunnel on the pinky side.

kidTest.q: What can happen if a nerve in a tunnel is squeezed?
kidTest.explain: A pinched nerve makes fingers tingle, like a sleeping foot.

kidTest.q: The carpal ___ is a groove with a roof on the palm side of your wrist. (t _ _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: It is called the carpal tunnel.

advancedTest.q: A cyclist has weak finger spreading and adductor pollicis but normal hypothenar strength and normal little-finger sensation. The likely lesion is:
choices: Zone 1 of Guyon's canal, before the nerve divides
Ulnar nerve at the elbow in the cubital tunnel
Deep motor branch distal to the hypothenar branches
Zone 3, affecting the superficial sensory branch
advancedTest.explain: A pure motor deficit that spares the hypothenar muscles points to the deep branch beyond its hypothenar twigs (a Zone 2 lesion). Zone 1 would also cause sensory loss.

advancedTest.q: Why is clawing often worse in a distal ulnar lesion than at the elbow?
choices: Lumbricals to the index finger are lost
Distal lesions also damage the median nerve
FDP to the ring and little fingers remains active
advancedTest.explain: This is the ulnar paradox: intact FDP flexes the fingertips while the intrinsics are paralyzed, which exaggerates the claw.

advancedTest.q: After a scapholunate ligament tear, the lunate follows the triquetrum into extension. This is best described as:
advancedTest.explain: Without the SL link, the scaphoid flexes and the lunate extends, giving the DISI pattern. VISI follows lunotriquetral injury.

advancedTest.q: A patient has median-distribution numbness that includes the thenar eminence and worsens with forearm use. This favors:
advancedTest.explain: The palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist, so thenar sensory loss points to a lesion above the tunnel, such as pronator syndrome.

lessons.title: Intrinsic Hand Muscles, Tendon Sheaths & Precision Grip

levels.kid:
Your hand has two teams of muscles. The big, strong team lives in your forearm and pulls on long strings called **tendons**, like a puppeteer pulling puppet strings. That team gives you a strong grip, like holding a bat.

The second team is tiny and lives right inside your hand. These little muscles do the careful jobs: picking up a bead, turning a page, or writing your name.

Your thumb has its own special muscles. They let it swing across to touch each fingertip. That is a big reason humans are so good with tools!

The tendon strings slide inside slippery tubes called **sheaths**, like a straw around a string. The sheaths help the strings glide smoothly.
levels.hs:
Hand movements come from two groups of muscles. **Extrinsic** muscles start in the forearm and reach the hand through long tendons. **Intrinsic** muscles start and end inside the hand.

The intrinsic muscles form four groups:
- **Thenar muscles** make up the thumb's fleshy pad: abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis. They allow **opposition**, which means bringing the thumb across to meet the fingertips.
- **Hypothenar muscles** form the pad below the little finger.
- **Lumbricals** are four small muscles that bend the knuckles and straighten the finger joints together. That combination produces a flat "tabletop" position.
- **Interossei** sit between the long hand bones (metacarpals). The **palmar** interossei pull fingers together (adduct). The **dorsal** interossei spread them apart (abduct). A handy memory aid is PAD and DAB.

Two nerves control these muscles. The **median nerve** supplies the thenar muscles and the two lumbricals next to the thumb. The **ulnar nerve** supplies almost all the rest.

Flexor tendons glide inside **synovial sheaths**, which are fluid-filled tubes that cut friction. Fibrous bands called **pulleys** hold the tendons close to the bone.

**Power grip**, such as holding a hammer, relies mostly on the forearm flexors. **Precision grip**, such as holding a pencil, depends on the intrinsic muscles. An infection inside a tendon sheath, called **flexor tenosynovitis**, is a surgical emergency.
levels.college:
**Intrinsic hand muscles** are grouped by position and innervation.

- **Thenar group** (usually supplied by the **recurrent branch of the median nerve**, C8-T1): abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis (its deep head is often ulnar-supplied) and opponens pollicis. **Adductor pollicis** sits deep in the palm and belongs to the ulnar territory, supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
- **Hypothenar group** (deep branch of the ulnar nerve): abductor digiti minimi, flexor digiti minimi brevis and opponens digiti minimi. Palmaris brevis is superficial and supplied by the superficial branch of the ulnar nerve.
- **Lumbricals**: four muscles that arise from the **flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendons** and insert on the radial side of the **extensor expansion**. They flex the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints and extend the interphalangeal (IP) joints. Lumbricals 1-2 are supplied by the median nerve; 3-4 by the deep ulnar nerve.
- **Interossei**: there are 3 palmar interossei (adduct toward the axis of the middle finger) and 4 dorsal interossei (abduct). Both sets also flex the MCP joints and extend the IP joints through the extensor expansion. All are supplied by the deep ulnar nerve.

A useful rule is **"LOAF"**: the median nerve supplies Lumbricals 1-2, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis and Flexor pollicis brevis. The ulnar nerve supplies the remaining intrinsics.

**Tendon sheaths.** The thumb's flexor pollicis longus runs in the **radial bursa**. The **ulnar bursa** encloses the FDS and FDP tendons and usually continues into the little finger's digital sheath. The index, middle and ring fingers usually have separate digital sheaths. The **fibrous flexor sheath** contains five annular pulleys (A1-A5) and three cruciform pulleys (C1-C3). The **A2 and A4** pulleys are most important for preventing **bowstringing**. **Trigger finger** results from tendon catching at the A1 pulley.

**Grips.** Power grip involves the FDS and FDP plus wrist extensors, with the thumb acting as a clamp. Precision pinch requires thenar opposition, adductor pollicis stabilization and interosseous control.

**Kanavel's signs** of flexor sheath infection are: a finger held in a flexed posture, fusiform swelling, tenderness along the sheath, and pain on passive extension.
levels.phd:
Precision handling emerges from the coupling of intrinsic muscles to the **extensor mechanism**, which is a tendinous network rather than a single tendon. The extensor digitorum tendon divides into a **central slip**, which inserts on the base of the middle phalanx, and two **lateral bands**. The lateral bands receive interosseous and lumbrical contributions and converge as the **terminal tendon** on the distal phalanx. The **sagittal bands** center the tendon over the MCP joint. The **transverse retinacular ligaments** stop the lateral bands from slipping dorsally. The **oblique retinacular ligament** (Landsmeer) passes volar to the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) axis and dorsal to the distal interphalangeal (DIP) axis, and it helps coordinate PIP and DIP extension.

Intrinsic action at the MCP joint depends on joint position. Interosseous lines of action lie volar to the MCP axis, which makes them MCP flexors. Their pull on the lateral bands passes dorsal to the IP axes, which makes them IP extensors. The lumbrical is mechanically unique because it links a flexor (FDP) to an extensor. Its contraction pulls the FDP tendon distally, which relaxes flexor tension and so enables IP extension. Its high density of muscle spindles has led to the view that it acts partly as a **proprioceptive sensor**, although this remains debated.

**Thumb.** The **trapeziometacarpal** joint is a saddle joint with reciprocally concave-convex surfaces. Opposition combines abduction, flexion and pronation with axial rotation, and the opponens pollicis contributes much of the pronation. Adductor pollicis supplies key pinch force. **Froment's sign** reveals its paralysis: the patient substitutes the median-supplied flexor pollicis longus, so the IP joint flexes during pinch.

**Clawing** from ulnar palsy reflects intrinsic loss. The extrinsic extensor hyperextends the MCP joints, and the FDP flexes the IP joints. The **ulnar paradox** describes how a proximal ulnar lesion that also denervates the ulnar FDP produces less clawing than a distal lesion at the wrist.

**Variability.** The **Martin-Gruber** (forearm) and **Riche-Cannieu** (palm) median-ulnar connections are common. They can preserve thenar function after median injury and can confuse electrodiagnosis. Thenar innervation therefore cannot be assumed to be purely median. Napier's 1956 classification of grips into power and precision remains the foundational framework.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the intrinsic system is examined through a few dependable tests:
- **First dorsal interosseous** abduction against resistance, while palpating the muscle, is the most reliable ulnar motor test.
- **Abductor pollicis brevis** strength, tested by raising the thumb perpendicular to the palm, is the most reliable median motor test.
- Wasting in the **first web space** suggests ulnar neuropathy, C8-T1 radiculopathy, or motor neuron disease. **Split hand** wasting, where thenar and first dorsal interosseous muscles waste more than hypothenar muscles, is characteristic of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

**Intrinsic tightness** is assessed with the **Bunnell test**. The examiner checks PIP flexion with the MCP joint extended and then flexed. Flexion that is restricted only when the MCP joint is extended indicates intrinsic tightness. This is common after crush injury, in compartment syndrome of the hand, and in rheumatoid disease. The hand has about 10 compartments, and decompression requires dorsal interosseous, thenar and hypothenar incisions; forearm fasciotomy alone is not enough.

Positioning to prevent contracture uses the **intrinsic-plus** ("safe") position: MCP joints flexed to about 70-90 degrees and IP joints extended. This keeps the collateral ligaments at their full length.

**Flexor tendon surgery** has advanced considerably:
- In **zone II**, the former "no man's land" where both FDS and FDP run inside the sheath, multistrand core sutures support early active motion protocols.
- **WALANT** (wide-awake local anesthesia, no tourniquet) lets surgeons watch active gliding during the operation.
- Partial venting of the A2 or A4 pulley is now accepted when it improves gliding.

In **pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis**, *Staphylococcus aureus* is the usual organism. Spread between the thumb and little-finger sheaths through **Parona's space** produces a **horseshoe abscess**. Treatment combines sheath irrigation with antibiotics.

For **nerve palsy reconstruction**, tendon transfers such as the Camitz or Huber opponensplasty, and Zancolli lasso procedures for clawing, restore function. **Distal nerve transfer**, such as the anterior interosseous nerve to the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve in proximal ulnar injury, aims to reinnervate the intrinsics before motor end-plates degenerate, usually within about 12-18 months. Debated questions include supercharge end-to-side outcomes and how well cortical remapping supports functional precision.

keyPoints: Intrinsic muscles: thenar, hypothenar, lumbricals, interossei, adductor pollicis
LOAF muscles are median; nearly all other intrinsics are ulnar
Palmar interossei adduct (PAD), dorsal interossei abduct (DAB)
Lumbricals and interossei flex the MCP and extend the IP joints via the extensor expansion
A2 and A4 pulleys prevent bowstringing; trigger finger involves A1
Kanavel's signs identify flexor sheath infection, a surgical emergency

test.q: Which nerve supplies the interossei?
test.explain: All interossei are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

test.q: Dorsal interossei mainly produce which finger movement?
test.explain: DAB: Dorsal ABduct. Palmar interossei adduct.

test.q: The lumbricals arise from the tendons of which muscle?
test.explain: Lumbricals originate on the FDP tendons and insert on the extensor expansion.

test.q: Which muscle is supplied by the ulnar nerve rather than the median?
test.explain: Adductor pollicis is ulnar; the others belong to the median nerve's LOAF group.

test.q: Lumbricals act on the finger joints by:
choices: Flexing both MCP and IP joints
Flexing MCP joints and extending IP joints
Extending MCP joints and flexing IP joints
Extending both MCP and IP joints
test.explain: They flex the MCP and extend the IP joints, producing the tabletop position.

test.q: Which pulleys are most important for preventing bowstringing?
test.explain: The A2 and A4 pulleys are the critical ones. A1 is the pulley involved in trigger finger.

test.q: The flexor pollicis longus tendon runs within the:
test.explain: The radial bursa surrounds the FPL tendon; the ulnar bursa encloses the FDS and FDP tendons.

test.q: Which is one of Kanavel's signs?
test.explain: The four signs are flexed posture, fusiform swelling, sheath tenderness and pain on passive extension.

test.q: Holding a pencil is an example of a grip that depends mainly on:
test.explain: Precision grip relies on the intrinsic muscles; power grip relies mostly on the forearm flexors.

test.q: Bringing the thumb across the palm to touch the fingertips is called ___.
test.explain: Opposition is driven by the thenar muscles, especially opponens pollicis.

test.q: Trigger finger involves tendon catching at which pulley?
test.explain: The A1 pulley sits over the MCP joint.

test.q: Muscles that start and end within the hand are called ___ muscles.
test.explain: Extrinsic muscles, by contrast, start in the forearm.

kidTest.q: Where do the tiny careful hand muscles live?
kidTest.explain: The small muscles for careful jobs sit right inside the hand.

kidTest.q: What are the long strings that muscles pull on?
kidTest.explain: Tendons connect muscles to bones.

kidTest.q: What does the thumb do that helps us use tools?
choices: It grows longer as we grip things
It bends backward to brace the hand
kidTest.explain: The thumb swings across the palm to meet each of the other fingertips, which lets us grip and handle tools.

kidTest.q: Which job needs the tiny hand muscles most?
kidTest.explain: Careful jobs use the tiny muscles; strong grips use the forearm team.

kidTest.q: Tendons slide in slippery tubes called s _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Sheaths help tendons glide smoothly.

advancedTest.q: Why does a wrist-level ulnar lesion claw more than an elbow-level lesion?
choices: The lumbricals regain median supply after the lesion
The ulnar FDP is spared, so IP flexion stays strong
The radial nerve takes over the hand intrinsics
The extensor tone is reduced at the wrist level
advancedTest.explain: This is the ulnar paradox. A proximal lesion also weakens the ulnar FDP, which reduces IP flexion and so lessens clawing.

advancedTest.q: On the Bunnell test, PIP flexion is limited only with the MCP joint extended. This indicates:
advancedTest.explain: MCP extension stretches the intrinsics. Restriction that depends on MCP position points to intrinsic tightness.

advancedTest.q: After a complete median nerve transection, thenar function is preserved. The best explanation is:
choices: FPL tenodesis acting on the thumb
Lumbrical substitution for the thenar muscles
Radial nerve sprouting into the palm
advancedTest.explain: A Riche-Cannieu median-ulnar connection can give the ulnar nerve control of the thenar muscles.

advancedTest.q: Why is the intrinsic-plus position used for splinting?
choices: It relaxes the median nerve in the carpal tunnel
It keeps the collateral ligaments at full length
It unloads the A1 pulley under tension
It shortens the lateral bands to aid healing
advancedTest.explain: Flexed MCP and extended IP joints keep the collateral ligaments stretched, which prevents stiffness.
